cultivar: Mengku large-leaf (Mengku dayezhong), a nationally registered Yunnan assamica population
processing: Raw pu-erh: pan-fired, rolled and sun-dried maocha, pressed into cakes; the thick Mengku leaf tolerates a firmer roll and a tighter press than Yiwu leaf.
harvest_season: Spring (late March to April) is the main harvest; autumn (guhua) tea is popular locally for its softer, more fragrant style.
appearance_dry: Broad, thick, dark-green leaves with large fuzzy buds and sturdy stems, pressed into a firm cake.
appearance_liquor: Bright golden-yellow, deepening to orange-gold with age, clear.
appearance_wet: Big, thick, very supple leaves with fat buds; the largest leaf of any common pu-erh origin.
taste_profile: High floral and grassy fragrance, a decisive bitterness that converts fast into a long sweetness, a thick body and a fresh, slightly cooling finish; the archetype of the Lincang style.

brewing.notes: Rinse once. The big leaf takes a moment to open, so the first steep can run a touch longer than for Yiwu; after that keep them short, as Mengku bitterness builds quickly.

vintage_note: Sold by spring harvest year and by village or garden, from loose maocha and boutique cakes up to the large standardised cakes of the Shuangjiang Mengku Tea Company (Rongshi brand), which carry a production year like a factory cake. Young (1–3 years) Mengku is bright and bitter; mid-aged (5–15 years) it turns honeyed and floral, and the early-2000s Rongshi cakes are the usual example of what the region does with time. Most supply is 2005–2025 and mostly dry-stored in Lincang or Kunming; it is a tea that ages lighter and more fragrant than Menghai tea rather than darker and heavier.
description:
Mengku is a town and basin in Shuangjiang County, Lincang, split by the Nanmeng river into an east half and a west half of tea mountains, and it gives its name to the Mengku large-leaf variety that grows across the region. It is the engine room of Lincang pu-erh: famous villages such as Bingdao, Xiaohusai, Dahusai, Bawai and Nuowu are all Mengku villages, and the Mengku Daxueshan wild tea forest above the basin is one of the largest stands of old wild tea trees known.

The leaf is huge, thick and bud-rich, and it is processed the standard sheng way: wok firing, rolling, sun drying and pressing. The big local company, Shuangjiang Mengku Tea (Rongshi), makes factory-scale cakes from this material, while hundreds of small producers sell village maocha and small-run cakes.

The cup is the Lincang signature: lifted floral and grassy aroma, a frank bitterness that turns to sweetness within a few seconds, a thick soup and a clean cooling finish. It is less heavy and less tobacco-like than Menghai tea and more fragrant, and it drinks well young. Brew it with short steeps after a slightly longer opening infusion; overleafing brings out the bitter side before the sweetness has a chance.

Sold by spring year and village. Prices range from reasonable blends of the basin to luxury single-garden tea, with Bingdao at the top. The region's weak spot is honesty about tree age: 'Mengku gushu' is a very common wrapper and a lot of it is young-tree or terrace tea from the lower slopes, so buy on the thickness of the body and the length of the sweetness rather than the word.

If you like Mengku and want to taste the regional extremes, try Bingdao (pure sweetness) and Xiaohusai (big, fragrant, more bitter) side by side.
